\chapter{Evening}
\label{ch:ml-evening}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say evening in Malayalam with vaikunnēraṁ, 'latening time'.}

Say vaikunnēraṁ, trace it to vaikuka 'to get late', and flag that sources disagree on whether it also covers afternoon.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}]{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} (vaikunnēraṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} built from a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to get late\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C27-vaikunneram}



\begin{quote}
Telugu reached for Sanskrit to name the evening. Malayalam's most common word takes a completely different route — an everyday verb, not a borrowed noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}} (\textbf{vaikunnēraṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{evening}\textquotedblright{} — is, per Wiktionary, a compound: \textbf{\ml{വൈക്}} (\emph{vaikŭ}) + \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}} (\emph{-uṁ}) + \textbf{\ml{നേരം}} (\emph{nēraṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}\textquotedblright{}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{latening time}.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\ml{നേരം}} is itself confirmed native \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} (cognate Tamil \ta{நேரம்}), not a Sanskrit borrowing — so unlike Telugu's Sanskrit \textbf{\te{సాయంత్రం}}, this whole compound is native Dravidian, start to finish. The \textbf{\ml{വൈക്}} root plausibly connects to an everyday Malayalam verb, \textbf{\ml{വൈകുക}} (\emph{vaikuka}), confirmed \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to get late}\textquotedblright{} — though be honest that this specific link is the author's own reasonable inference, not something Wiktionary's compound entry states outright.

\begin{culture}
Here's a real tension, not smoothed over: Wiktionary's own entry lists \textbf{both} \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} \textbf{and} \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} as senses of this single word. But two independently-fetched phrasebook sources (ling-app.com, talkpal.ai) draw a cleaner line — \textbf{evening} is \textbf{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}}, while \textbf{afternoon} gets its own, separate compound built on \textbf{\ml{ഉച്ച}} (already met, Chapter 17, \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\ml{കഴിഞ്ഞ്}} (\emph{kazhinju}, \textquotedblleft{}passed, gone by\textquotedblright{}). This project's discipline is to flag genuine disagreement rather than quietly pick whichever source is more convenient — so treat the afternoon/evening boundary here as \textbf{genuinely blurry} in the dictionary sense, even though the two everyday phrasebook sources agree on a cleaner practical split.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vaikunnēraṁ\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}latening time\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday verb root — vaikuka, \textquotedblleft{}to get late\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest tension — Wiktionary blurs afternoon/evening; phrasebooks split them cleanly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} literally mean, and what verb is it plausibly built from? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Latening time\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{\ml{വൈകുക}}, \textquotedblleft{}to get late.\textquotedblright{}) Do all sources agree on where \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} ends and \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} begins for this word? (\textbf{No} — Wiktionary lists it as covering both senses; phrasebook sources instead draw a clean line, treating afternoon as a separate compound.) Is \ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} a Sanskrit borrowing, like Telugu's \te{సాయంత్రం}? (\textbf{No} — it's a native Dravidian compound, built from an everyday verb and a native \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} word, \ml{നേരം}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
